Text is #0055ff on white, so foreground first.

**Not by klar's default measure.** `#0055ff` as text on `#ffffff` scores **4.3**, below the 4.5 needed for AA body text. I ran it as foreground on background, which is the direction that matters because OKCA is polarity-aware. The color is in sRGB gamut, so the number is reliable.

The two algorithms disagree:

| Algorithm | Ratio | AA body text (4.5) |
|---|---|---|
| OKCA (klar default) | 4.3 | Fails |
| Classic WCAG 2.x luminance (`--type wcag2`) | 5.6 | Passes |

- **OKCA:** it is the project's tool default and models perceived contrast, so I'd treat 4.3 as the answer.
- **WCAG 2.x:** if a compliance audit is judged strictly on the formal WCAG 2.x formula, 5.6 technically passes. The two figures still don't agree with each other.
- **Recommendation:** don't use `#0055ff` for body text unless the formal 2.x formula is the only bar. Reversed (white text on `#0055ff`), it scores 4.5 and passes.

I can run `klar find "#ffffff" "#0055ff" --target 4.5` for a slightly darker blue that passes under OKCA, along with how far it drifts from the original. Want me to?

There's no pass that keeps the brand green's saturation. The closest one that passes is **`#047f38`**, but it costs a visible shift, so that's your call.

**Where `#22c55e` stands.** On white it scores 1.9 OKCA, and body text needs 4.5. Darkening it alone tops out at 2.2. At this hue (about 150°) and saturation (chroma 0.19), the color can't get dark enough to reach 4.5 without losing saturation. `klar find` exited 1 with `lightness-exhausted` and did not apply a fix.

**The candidate that passes.** With `--allow-desaturation`, `klar find` returns `#047f38`:

| | `#22c55e` (brand) | `#047f38` (candidate) |
|---|---|---|
| OKLCH lightness | 0.72 | 0.52 |
| OKLCH chroma | 0.19 | 0.14 |
| OKLCH hue | 149.6° | 149.7° |
| OKCA on white (text on background) | 1.9 | **4.6** (passes AA body text) |

- **Drift:** deltaE is 22 from the brand green. The playbook scale calls that "very different". Hue is preserved, but the color reads as a noticeably deeper, duller green.
- **Margin:** 4.6 clears 4.5 by only 0.1. It is the minimal fix, not a comfortable one.

**Options:**
1. **Adopt `#047f38` for body text only.** Keep `#22c55e` for fills, buttons and large text. Large text (24px and up) needs only 3.0, which the brand green (1.9) also misses. Non-text UI has the same 3.0 threshold.
2. **Don't use the brand green as text on white.** Put it on a dark background instead, or use a near-black text color and keep the green as an accent.

I haven't changed any token files. If you pick option 1, I can add it as a text-specific token.

final:
I wrote `audit.sh` and ran it. 3 of the 6 foreground tokens pass AA body text (4.5 or higher) on the `#ffffff` background. The script exits 1 because of the failures, so it will fail a CI job.

| Token | Result | OKCA ratio |
|---|---|---|
| text-primary | PASS | 14.8 |
| text-muted | FAIL | 4.0 |
| brand | PASS | 5.0 |
| success | FAIL | 2.0 (outside sRGB) |
| danger | FAIL | 2.8 (outside sRGB) |
| accent | PASS | 6.4 |

- **text-muted:** it misses by 0.5. A lightness nudge should probably fix it, and `klar find "#ffffff" "oklch(0.55 0.02 260)" --target 4.5` will propose one.
- **success and danger:** both are authored outside sRGB. The chroma values (0.3 and 0.26) can't be displayed, so klar measured the nearest displayable colors, `#00c248` and `#fd0025`. The ratios above describe those colors, not the tokens as written.
  - Lowering chroma won't change the number until the color is back in gamut.
  - Lightness alone likely can't fix `success`. Green at this chroma tops out well below 4.5, so it probably needs a different color.

The script follows the klar playbook:
- **Argument order:** it runs `klar contrast <fg> <bg>`, foreground first. OKCA is polarity-aware, so the reverse order gives different numbers.
- **Out-of-gamut tokens:** klar exits 1 for these. The call is guarded, so `set -euo pipefail` doesn't abort the run partway. Those tokens are labeled in their result line.
- **Dependencies:** it puts `node_modules/.bin` on the PATH and needs `jq`, which is installed here.

An out-of-gamut token that passed would still count as a pass, with only the note attached. If you'd rather fail CI on any out-of-gamut token, that's a one-line change.

The two colors now share a chroma of about 0.20, and neither one passes 3:1 as large text on white.

`klar match` moved the blue and left the coral alone:

| Token | Final hex | OKCA on white (text on background) | Large text (3:1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blue | **#3481fd** (was #3b82f6) | 2.9 | Fails, 0.1 short |
| Coral | **#e94560** (unchanged) | 2.8 | Fails, 0.2 short |

- **Match:** Blue's chroma went from 0.19 to 0.20 to match the coral, with the same hue and lightness. The change is a deltaE of 1, which is imperceptible.
- **Contrast:** I measured each color as foreground on `#ffffff`, since OKCA depends on which color is the text. Both exited 0, so the figures describe the colors as authored.
- **Original blue:** I didn't measure #3b82f6 on white, so I can't say whether the match made blue's contrast better or worse.

Neither accent works as large text on white. To fix that, run `klar find "#ffffff" <color> --target 3` on each and check the deltaE cost before adopting the result. Say if you want me to do that.

Yes, it's a visible change, though it's still recognisably the same coral-red. The deltaE between `#e94560` and `#bf103f` is **13**.

By the playbook's scale, 11–20 is "clearly different". That's distinct enough to tell apart at a glance, but well short of a different color. Only the 0–5 range would be a barely noticeable nudge.

| | Lightness | Chroma | Hue |
|---|---|---|---|
| `#e94560` | 0.63 | 0.20 | 15.73 |
| `#bf103f` | 0.52 | 0.20 | 15.79 |

- **Lightness:** it dropped by about 0.11. This is the whole change, and it reads as a darker, deeper coral.
- **Hue and chroma:** both are essentially unchanged, so the color hasn't shifted toward orange or purple. It also hasn't gone duller.
- **Contrast on white:** the OKCA ratio went from 2.8 (fails) to 4.7 (passes AA body text at 4.5). I measured both as text on `#ffffff`.

The result is the same color, only darker. It will look richer and less bright next to the old one. If the coral is used as a large fill, brand mark or illustration, the designer may want to check it against the brand feel. If it's mostly text or UI accents, the change should be fine.

The 4.7 leaves little margin above 4.5. It's the same fix `klar find` produces, so the designer picked the lightest passing option.
